study.title: 1 Kings 6 - The building of the temple and the presence of God among the people
study.overview: The chapter narrates the construction of Solomon's temple, from the beginning of the works to the completion of the work. The text highlights the order, the artisanal care, the symbolic wealth of the sanctuary and, above all, the word of the Lord to Solomon in the midst of the construction: the building would only make sense if it came accompanied by obedience. Thus, the temple is not only a monumental work, but the place prepared for God's presence among Israel, with covenant and holiness at the centre.

outline.title: Beginning of the work and external description of the temple
outline.explanation: The chapter begins by placing the construction in the fourth year of Solomon's reign and describes measurements, portico, windows, side chambers and the silent mode of the building. The detail emphasizes planning, order and reverence, because the stones were already prepared and there was no tool noise on site.

outline.title: The word of the Lord and the consecrated interior
outline.explanation: In the midst of the work, God speaks to Solomon and conditions the permanence of his promise to obedience to his commandments. Then, the text describes the coating of cedar and gold, the inner compartment and the most holy place, where the ark would be placed, emphasizing the distinction between the common and the holy space.

outline.title: Querubins, ornamentation and completion of construction
outline.explanation: The chapter details the cherubim, the carved figures, the gates, the inner atrium and, finally, informs that the house was finished in seven years. The visual and symbolic richness points to the glory and holiness of the God who dwells in the midst of his people.

study.context: The text mentions Solomon's fourth year and the beginning in the month of Zip, and the end in the month of Bul. Commentator notes associate this data with an ancient chronology of Israel, but also recognize differences between chronological proposals. The immediate context of the chapter is the expansion of Solomon's royal project, with the temple as the central construction of the account.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the presence of God in the midst of his people is a gift of the covenant, but is not treated as something automatic or merely architectural. The divine promise in 11-13 unites temple and obedience: the sanctuary is a sign of the Lord's faithfulness, but the permanence of this experience depends on walking in the statutes of God. The most holy place, the ark, the gold and the cherubim communicate holiness, separation and glory, remembering that God is accessible, but not common. The silence of the work and careful preparation also reinforce that service to God must be done with reverence, order and excellence. At the same time, the text does not transform the building to an ultimate end; it points to the God who promises to inhabit among Israel and not abandon his people.

scholarViews.insight: The temple is presented as the house where God met with his people, with a plant that resembles the tabernacle, but on a larger scale.
The house of the Lord is described as directed and shaped by God, and is dedicated to his honor and service.
The temple was completed in the eleventh year of Solomon in the eighth month after seven years of construction.

questions: What does Solomon's obedience have to do with God's promise to dwell among Israel?
Why does the text emphasize both beauty, gold and temple details rather than just say that it was built?
How can the silent and prepared construction of the stones guide our posture in Christian service today?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to treat worship with reverence and life with obedience. The practical application is to examine whether our search for visible forms of spirituality is accompanied by concrete fidelity to God's commandments. It is also an invitation to serve with excellence and without ostentation, remembering that the value of work is not in the noise, but in fidelity to the Lord. If God desires to dwell among his people, then the life of the people must reflect holiness, order, and submission to his word.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided differ in chronological questions and mention different estimates for the period of Exodus and the date of the temple; therefore, the abstract avoids setting dates as an undeniable fact. It is also not possible to safely identify all materials and measurements according to modern equivalence, so such details were kept only at the descriptive level of the biblical text and notes. The interpretations of commentators were presented as readings, not as definitive conclusions of the chapter.
